messages.subject: [statnet_help] Simmelian statistics
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I was trying to fit models with simmelian and simmelianties statistics. It
turns out that the model with simmelian statistics was a good fit, however
this particular statistic was not significant. On the other hand, model
with simmelianties was slightly better fit and this time simmelianties
statistic was statistically significant.

I was wondering what would be the difference in the interpretation of these
two statistics. I understand Simmel's theory and how Krackhardt defines
super-strong ties, however not sure what would be the difference between
these two statistics.

Best,
Srecko

messages.body_plain:
Thank you for the prompt response.

Of course. The current problematic model is below. It was selected from a
large set of models and demonstrated the best fit in a short run (that
actually completed). But please note that this is not the only
model/network for which I have run into this problem -- the model selection
process iterated through a large set of combinations of the GW-terms. Also,
the Monte Carlos we have run is much simpler, including gwesp() as the only
structural term.

    ergm(lc.ntwk.memberorg.na ~ edges
         + gwesp(0.25, fix=TRUE)
         + gwdsp(0.00, fix=TRUE)
         + gwdegree(0.25, fix=TRUE)
         + nodematch("budget.cat5",    diff=TRUE)
         + nodematch("employees.cat5", diff=TRUE)
         + nodematch("salesall.cat5",  diff=TRUE)
         + nodematch("founded.cat5",   diff=TRUE)
         + nodematch("members.cat5",   diff=TRUE)
         + nodematch("plantsize.cat5", diff=TRUE)
         + nodematch("sic861", diff=FALSE, keep = 1)
         + nodematch("sic862", diff=FALSE, keep = 1)
         + nodematch("sic863", diff=FALSE, keep = 1)
         + nodematch("sic864", diff=FALSE, keep = 1)
         + nodematch("sic865", diff=FALSE, keep = 1)
         + nodematch("sic866", diff=FALSE, keep = 1)
         + nodematch("sic869", diff=FALSE, keep = 1),
         verbose=TRUE,
         control=control.ergm(
             MCMLE.maxit=20,
             MCMC.interval=2048,
             MCMC.samplesize=2^12))

messages.body_plain:
Sorry, Martina, I wasn't clear.

Of the 511 specifications I tried, this was the model that performed the
best *and* completed in 5 iterations (all else was held at the default
values for these preliminary runs). Many models didn't complete at all in
12 hours. I haven't done a full tally to determine why some didn't complete
(some were probably very bad models), but of the 511, there were 279 that
did not produce MCMC diagnostics or GOF plots because the ergm() failed in
one way or another.

messages.subject: [statnet_help] ergm(): Stuck Estimation
messages.body_plain:
There are two general paths to follow:

1. data/model issues

* for all of the networks, take a look at some descriptive stats

size & density of network -- if too small or too dense/too sparse, 
you may not be able to identify this many effects.

summary statistics for all of the model terms (summary(net ~ terms), low 
values can be a problem, but so can maximum values)

* make sure all of your nodematch terms are using categorical attributes 
(not quantitative covariates).

* remove the gw*sp terms, if you still have a problem, this suggests 
something very basic is wrong.  put them back one at a time (only gwesp, 
then only gwnsp, then both), see if there's a pattern in when the problem 
emerges.

* for the models that converged, take a look at

the MCMC diagnostics (slow mixing in traceplot indicative of a problem)

parameter correlations (in the ergm fit object, high correlations a 
problem)


2. code bugs (if you don't find anything from the above)

install an earlier version of ergm and see if you get different results.

best,
mm

Could anyone give me some advice on this?

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I am seeking to calculate eigenvector centrality of all nodes for a
directed, weighted network. My empirical network also has some missing edge
data in which I do not know whether or not a tie was formed between nodes.

My understanding is that I can do this by using the evcent() function in
"sna" and specifying gmode="digraph. Although there is not an option in the
parameters of evcent(), I believe that this automatically calculates the
*out-*eigenvector centrality, whereas transposing the weighted adjacency
matrix and running the same function will calculate the *in-*eigenvector
centrality of nodes. The following code gives an example of this:

##
> library(statnet)
> g <- network(rgraph(20, tprob=.4), directed=T)   #generate sample network
> g %e% "weight" <- sample(1:10, network.edgecount(g), replace=T)   # add
edge weights
> g[c(sample(1:network.size(g), 5)), c(sample(1:network.size(g), 5))] <- NA
  #add some NAs randomly

> sna::evcent(as.sociomatrix(g, attr="weight"), rescale=F, gmode="digraph")
  # calculate out-eigenvector centrality?
> sna::evcent(t(as.sociomatrix(g, attr="weight")), rescale=F,
gmode="digraph") # calculate in-eigenvector centrality?
##

I have 3 main questions:

1) Could someone please help me verify whether my understanding of how to
calculate in vs. out-eigenvector centrality is correct and if the procedure
I am implementing above is valid?

2) In order to calculate a "total" eigenvector centrality for the directed
graph, would it be reasonable to sum the upper and lower triangles of the
directed adjacency matrix, create a symmetric (undirected) matrix from the
result and calculate eigenvector centrality as you would for an undirected
graph?

3) Finally, I have run some simple tests of missing values and it appears
as though they are being handled reasonably, although I lack a good
mechanistic understanding of how they are being treated. Thus, I would also
be very grateful is anyone here could provide a simplified description of
how missing values are handled in evcent() or point me to some material to
help me understand. Available literature (
http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0378873305000353) seems
to suggest that centrality measures are relatively robust to a low
proportion of missing edge data.

My apologies for the long message and thank you in advance for the
continued help,

Tom

> directed, weighted network. My empirical network also has some missing 
> edge data in which I do not know whether or not a tie was formed 
> between nodes.
>
> My understanding is that I can do this by using the evcent() function 
> in "sna" and specifying gmode="digraph. Although there is not an 
> option in the parameters of evcent(), I believe that this 
> automatically calculates the *out-*eigenvector centrality, whereas 
> transposing the weighted adjacency matrix and running the same 
> function will calculate the *in-*eigenvector centrality of nodes. The 
> following code gives an example of this:
>
Yes, although you should be careful about interpreting the principal 
eigenvector of a directed graph.  It is not meaningless, but can do 
things you might not expect; a slightly different index like the 
Katz/Bonacich power/Salancik family may prove more useful (although 
these do not always have solutions in the directed case).  (This is 
among the many things that sna lets you compute under the assumption 
that you know what you are doing, whether or not it is necessarily a 
good idea in any given setting.)

>
> I have 3 main questions:
>
> 1) Could someone please help me verify whether my understanding of how 
> to calculate in vs. out-eigenvector centrality is correct and if the 
> procedure I am implementing above is valid?
>

See above.  Also, if your system isn't too big, you may want to force 
the use of eigen() with use.eigen in this case; the default algorithm 
scales much, much better, but is less numerically stable. This could 
matter here.

> 2) In order to calculate a "total" eigenvector centrality for the 
> directed graph, would it be reasonable to sum the upper and lower 
> triangles of the directed adjacency matrix, create a symmetric 
> (undirected) matrix from the result and calculate eigenvector 
> centrality as you would for an undirected graph?
>

You will want to think about why you want the eigenvector centrality, 
and about which network will give you the interpretation you require; 
what you suggest is one thing that one may do, but it is impossible to 
know whether it is appropriate without understanding the details of the 
problem.

> 3) Finally, I have run some simple tests of missing values and it 
> appears as though they are being handled reasonably, although I lack a 
> good mechanistic understanding of how they are being treated. Thus, I 
> would also be very grateful is anyone here could provide a simplified 
> description of how missing values are handled in evcent() or point me 
> to some material to help me understand. Available literature 
> (http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0378873305000353) 
> seems to suggest that centrality measures are relatively robust to a 
> low proportion of missing edge data.
>

evcent() will handle NAs by dropping the associated edges (i.e., 
treating the cell values as 0s).  I would suggest doing some quick 
robustness checks by randomly varying the states of the missing cells 
(e.g., by randomly drawing values from the edge value distribution 
(including 0s)) and recomputing to ensure that the missing data is not 
driving your results; as you note, this is a very robust measure, so you 
may find that the missing edge states make little difference.  If you 
need to do something more principled about the missing edge values, the 
obvious alternative is to use model-based imputation (here, using a 
valued ERGM).  This is considerably more involved, so I wouldn't 
recommend it for this purpose unless your robustness checks are telling 
you that you need it.

> continued help,

Hope that helps,
